Hyperoglyphe antarctica, commonly known as the Antarctic butterfish, exhibits several life-history traits typical of a large, slow-growing perciform. Field surveys have estimated that newly emerged yolk-sac larvae possess a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00022 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00022 grams], a remarkably modest starting mass that reflects the small diameter of the pelagic eggs. At a stable water temperature of 11.6 °C [T = 11.6 °C], these prolarvae hatch after an incubation period of approximately 18 days [ab = approximately 18 days], a duration that aligns with the developmental rates of other centrolophid species under similar thermal regimes. This brief lecithotrophic phase is critical for early survival, as the yolk-dependent alevins rely entirely on endogenous reserves before their mouths open and first exogenous feeding begins. The transition to exotrophic nutrition marks a precarious period of high mortality, a common bottleneck for ichthyoplankton in temperate waters.

As juveniles grow and accumulate body mass, their allometric scaling of length to weight follows a predictable power relationship. From field-collected specimens, the relationship between total length and wet weight has been used to estimate that a fish reaching the asymptotic or ultimate total length of 140 centimeters [Li = 140 centimeters] would achieve an ultimate wet weight of roughly 40,000 grams [Wwi = roughly 40,000 grams]. This extremely large adult body size places Hyperoglyphe antarctica among the heavier members of its family, a status that carries significant metabolic and energetic consequences. The progression from a larval mass of less than a milligram to a mature mass exceeding forty kilograms represents an extraordinary increase of several orders of magnitude, achieved over a prolonged growing period. Such a growth trajectory necessitates high ingestion rates during the juvenile stage to fuel the rapid deposition of somatic tissue, particularly in the pre-pubertal phase when daily energetic demands of tissue upkeep are most intense relative to body size.

Reproductive maturation in this species is characterized by a specific body size threshold rather than by age alone. Data from trawl surveys indicate that the length at which 50 percent of individuals attain sexual maturity, defined here as the total length at puberty, is 70.6 centimeters [Lp = 70.6 centimeters]. This measurement suggests that individuals must more than double their length from a typical juvenile size before they begin vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis. Achieving this substantial body length requires several years of sustained feeding and growth, effectively delaying the onset of gonad maturation until a size refuge from predation is likely achieved. The relatively large size at maturity compared to the ultimate length implies a reproductive strategy where females allocate considerable resources to somatic growth before investing heavily in egg production. This pattern is consistent with that observed in other long-lived, iteroparous teleosts inhabiting deep continental slope environments.

Fecundity estimates for Hyperoglyphe antarctica, derived from gravid females captured during the winter spawning season, reveal a high reproductive output consistent with a pelagic spawning strategy. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of 11.6 °C [T = 11.6 °C], females produce approximately 3,397 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3,397 eggs per spawning event] and are capable of completing roughly one spawning event per day [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per day] during the peak of the season. This high frequency of gamete release, paired with a comparatively modest clutch size per event, suggests that the species relies on a protracted spawning period and the repeated liberation of small batches of pelagic eggs to maximize total annual fecundity. The strategy contrasts with that of nest-guarding species that produce fewer, larger clutches and expend considerable parental effort. Such iterative spawning is common among commercially valuable slope-dwelling species and buffers against interannual variability in oceanographic conditions affecting larval survival.

The longevity of Hyperoglyphe antarctica has been estimated through otolith increment analysis, which provides a record of age and growth. The maximum lifespan for this species, recorded in a population inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature of 11.6 °C [T = 11.6 °C], has been placed at approximately 80 years [am = approximately 80 years]. This extreme longevity, comparable to that of some deep-sea rockfishes, positions the Antarctic butterfish as one of the longest-lived fishes in the Southern Ocean. Such a protracted lifespan, combined with a late age at puberty implied by a 70.6 centimeter length threshold, indicates a very slow life history pace that renders the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation. The trade-off between extended somatic persistence and a relatively modest per-event fecundity defines its demographic profile, and any increase in adult mortality from fishing pressure could rapidly erode the spawning stock biomass, given the low natural replacement rate of this long-lived teleost.
